newsitem.title: CHINA: China says HK demonstrations not Beijing business.
newsitem.headline: China says HK demonstrations not Beijing business.

text.p: China declined on Wednesday to comment on a pledge by Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa to protect the right to protest after the British colony's handover, saying such matters were none of Beijing's business.

"Beijing is responsible for the defence and foreign affairs of Hong Kong after it returns to Chinese rule," an official of the Hong Kong Macau Affairs Office under the State Council, or cabinet, said.
"Everything else is the responsibility of the government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region," he said.

In an interview on the ABC News programme "Nightline," Hong Kong's Tung pledged on Tuesday to protect the right to protest and vowed that no Tiananmen Square-style crackdown would take place under his leadership.

"Demonstration is part of our culture, demonstration is part of life... they will be free to demonstrate as they please, but I would hope they would abide by the laws of Hong Kong if they wish to do so," Tung said.
Rights groups and academics have warned of threats to freedom and civil liberties when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after 156 years under the British flag.

China maintains that it will abide by the "one country, two systems" formula for the return of Hong Kong that stipulates no change in the system in the booming capitalist city for 50 years after the handover.
Tung said anyone should "feel comfortable to demonstrate" after July 1, adding: "If they want to be martyrs, they will be very disappointed."

Asked if the 1989 crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square -- when Beijing crushed the student-led pro-democracy movement with heavy loss of life -- could be repeated in Hong Kong, Tung replied: "No, it can't happen here. It will not happen here. I will not allow it to happen here.

"Insofar as Hong Kong is concerned, we are living in a very different world, we have a culture which has demonstrations almost every day, we have people voicing different views everywhere," Tung said.
